name: LNK304DN-TL
title: LinkSwitch-TN LNK302/304-306: off-line switcher IC with a 700 V MOSFET for non-isolated supplies up to 360 mA
summary: A four-pin off-line converter chip that puts a 700 V power MOSFET, a 66 kHz oscillator with frequency jitter, on/off (cycle-skipping) control, cycle-by-cycle current limit, leading edge blanking, thermal shutdown and a high-voltage start-up supply on one die. It powers itself from its DRAIN pin, so no bias winding or bias supply is needed, and it is aimed at replacing linear and capacitor-dropper supplies in appliances, timers, LED drivers and industrial controls. It works in buck, buck-boost and flyback converters from 85 to 265 VAC and delivers from 63 mA (LNK302) to 360 mA (LNK306) in a buck. LNK304, LNK305 and LNK306 add auto-restart, which handles shorted outputs and open feedback loops; LNK302 does not have it.

circuits.title: Universal input, 12 V, 120 mA constant voltage buck supply
circuits.description: A non-isolated 1.44 W supply for appliance controls. RF1 limits inrush, filters differential noise and fuses the input; D3 and D4 rectify, and C4, L2 and C5 form a pi filter and bulk store. The LNK304 switches its SOURCE node, which is the converter's floating ground: D1 freewheels, L1 and C2 filter the output, and the design runs mostly discontinuous. D2 charges C3 to roughly the output voltage while D1 conducts, and R1 with R3 scale that to 1.65 V at FB. C1 holds the 5.8 V internal supply. R4 is a 3.3 kΩ pre-load; 2.4 kΩ in its place gives regulation down to zero load.
notes: D4 can be left out; fitting it improves EMI and line surge withstand.
C4 and C5 may sit between the LNK304 and the AC input to keep the switcher away from the input lines.

circuits.title: Typical buck converter
circuits.description: The basic high-side buck from a high-voltage DC input. The chip's SOURCE is the switching node; the freewheel diode and inductor make the buck stage, the output capacitor filters, and the diode-capacitor pair across the top samples the output for the FB divider. The BP capacitor holds the internal supply.

circuits.title: High-side buck, direct feedback
circuits.description: A step-down converter with the chip in the positive input line and its SOURCE as the switching node. D2 and C3 sample the output while D1 freewheels, and R1 with R3 bring that to the FB threshold. Output regulation is about ±10%; R4 provides the minimum load the direct feedback needs.

circuits.title: High-side buck, optocoupler feedback
circuits.description: The high-side buck with the output sensed by a Zener and an optocoupler. When the output exceeds the Zener voltage plus the LED drop, the LED lights and the phototransistor feeds current from BP into FB, skipping cycles. The resistor across the LED sets its bias. Accuracy depends on the reference, no pre-load is needed and no-load consumption is lowest.

circuits.title: Low-side buck, optocoupler feedback
circuits.description: A step-down converter with the chip in the negative input line, its SOURCE on -VIN and DRAIN as the switching node. The output sits between +VIN and the bottom of L1, negative with respect to +VIN. A Zener and optocoupler sense it and steer current from BP into FB. No pre-load is needed.

circuits.title: Low-side buck, constant current LED driver
circuits.description: The low-side buck driving LED strings from +VIN. The string current returns through R and L1 to DRAIN. The optocoupler LED sits across R, so it turns on when the drop across R reaches its forward voltage; R = VF / IO sets the output current. The phototransistor then feeds BP current into FB.

circuits.title: High-side buck-boost, direct feedback
circuits.description: An inverting converter with the chip in the positive line. When the MOSFET is on, L1 charges from SOURCE to -VIN; when off, it discharges through D1 into C2, giving an output negative with respect to +VIN that can be above or below the input. D2 and C3 sample the output for the R1-R3 divider at FB. A failed MOSFET does not put the input on the output. It needs an output load to hold regulation.

circuits.title: High-side buck-boost, constant current LED driver
circuits.description: The high-side buck-boost driving two strings of three LEDs. The LED current flows through D1 and RSENSE back to SOURCE; the 300 Ω and 2 kΩ resistors divide the voltage across RSENSE onto FB, so RSENSE = 2 V / IO sets the current. The 10 µF capacitor across RSENSE smooths the sensed voltage and the 100 nF capacitor across the strings filters the LED current. A failed MOSFET does not put the input on the LEDs.

circuits.title: Low-side buck-boost, optocoupler feedback
circuits.description: An inverting converter with the chip in the negative line, SOURCE on -VIN. L1 charges from +VIN through the MOSFET and discharges through D1 into C2, giving an output positive with respect to +VIN that can be above or below the input. A Zener and optocoupler sense it and steer BP current into FB. No pre-load is needed, a failed MOSFET does not put the input on the output, and no-load consumption is lowest.

operation.text: There is no pulse width modulation. Each cycle starts on the clock edge only if FB was below its threshold current; otherwise the whole cycle is skipped. The FB input is a source follower held at 1.65 V, and a current above 49 µA into the pin disables the next cycle. FB is sampled only at the start of the cycle and ignored for the rest of it. A switched cycle ends at the current limit or at DCMAX. Lighter load means more skipped cycles.

The oscillator averages 66 kHz and gives the DCMAX signal and the clock for each cycle. Its frequency is swept by about 4 kHz peak-to-peak at a 1 kHz rate, spreading conducted EMI for both average and quasi-peak limits; over the sweep the switching frequency moves between 64 kHz and 68 kHz. Jitter is observed on a scope triggered on the DRAIN falling edge.

While the MOSFET is off, a 5.8 V regulator charges the BP capacitor with current taken from DRAIN; while it is on, the chip runs from that capacitor. 0.1 µF is enough both to decouple and to store this energy. A 6.3 V shunt clamps BP when current is fed in through an external resistor, so the chip can be powered from a bias winding, which brings no-load input power down to about 50 mW.
The MOSFET is held off when BP falls under 4.85 V and is not enabled again until BP has climbed back to 5.8 V.
At a die temperature of 142 °C typical the MOSFET stops switching; it restarts after the die has cooled by 75 °C.

The MOSFET current is compared with ILIMIT each cycle and the switch turns off for the rest of the cycle once it is reached. For tLEB after turn-on the comparator is blanked, so the spike from capacitance and rectifier reverse recovery does not end the pulse early.

An oscillator-clocked counter is cleared each time FB is pulled high. If 50 ms pass without that, as with an overload, a shorted output or an open loop, switching stops for 800 ms, then tries again, repeating until the fault clears. Average output power in this state is about 6% of the maximum overload power. LNK302 has no auto-restart.

The output currents assume a buck converter, a minimum DC input of at least 70 V (input capacitance sized for it), KRP of 0.4 for CCM, 12 VDC out, 75% efficiency, a freewheel diode with trr ≤75 ns for MDCM or ≤35 ns for CCM, and the chip soldered to enough copper that the SOURCE pins stay at or below 100 °C.

MDCM generally gives the lowest cost and best efficiency. CCM always needs a larger inductor and an ultrafast (trr ≤35 ns) diode, so a larger device run in MDCM costs less than a smaller one in CCM; CCM is for when the highest output current is needed.

Ultrafast: trr ≤75 ns for MDCM at 70 °C ambient or below; trr ≤35 ns above 70 °C and for all CCM designs. A slower diode causes continuous conduction at start-up with large leading-edge current spikes that end cycles early and stop the output reaching regulation, or in CCM limit the power delivered. Fast-recovery and standard slow diodes are not to be used: their recovery current can overheat the diode or push the DRAIN current past its rating. UF400x parts suit MDCM designs at 70 °C ambient or below; for CCM or hotter designs a 35 ns diode such as the BYV26C.

An inexpensive standard-recovery part (1N400X series, for instance), specified glass passivated so its reverse recovery is defined. Its forward drop should be close to D1's so the voltage on C3 follows the output.

An off-the-shelf part with inductance at least the calculated typical value and an RMS rating at least the calculated RMS current. A single-ferrite drum or dog-bone (I-core) inductor is recommended for low cost and very low audible noise.
C2 smooths the inductor current. Output ripple is set mostly by its ESR rather than its capacitance.
Chosen so FB sits at 1.65 V at the target output. R3 is recommended as a 2 kΩ, 1% resistor, which biases the divider at about 0.8 mA for noise immunity.
A general-purpose part that charges to the output voltage while the switch is off and holds it as a sample. 10 µF to 22 µF; less capacitance gives poorer regulation at light load.

High-side direct-feedback designs whose load can fall under 3 mA need a pre-load giving at least 3 mA, so the inductor carries enough energy to pull the inductor end of C3 down to the input return through D2. In optocoupler designs the Zener or reference bias of 1 mA to 2 mA is the minimum load and prevents pulse bunching and higher ripple at zero load.

In buck and buck-boost circuits the SOURCE pins are the switching node: keep their copper as small as the thermal design allows to limit EMI. In a boost the SOURCE pins are on DC return and their copper can be made large for heat sinking. Keep the loop of the switcher, L1, D1 and C2 small. Place C1 next to the SOURCE and BYPASS pins. Keep the switcher away from the AC input lines; C4 and C5 can sit between them. In the recommended buck layouts (P or G package, and D package on the bottom side), the copper areas around the SOURCE pins are sized for heat sinking and EMI.

On the bench: the minimum DC input must stay above 70 VDC at full load and lowest line; peak DRAIN current must be below its rating at highest line, maximum overload just before auto-restart and highest ambient; the SOURCE pin temperature must be 100 °C or below at full power, lowest line and highest ambient, which leaves margin for RDS(ON) spread. Measure temperature with a battery-powered thermocouple meter, since SOURCE is a switching node, or raise the ambient to find the margin to thermal shutdown.

With SOURCE switching in buck and buck-boost circuits, ground the scope probe to a DC node such as the primary return or the DC input rail, never to SOURCE, and feed the supply from an isolated source such as an isolation transformer.
When FB is pulled low, switching resumes within tEN, at the next DCMAX rising edge (Figure 9); tP = 1/fOSC is the clock period.
No-load input power is typically 50 mW at 115 VAC and 80 mW at 230 VAC in a self-powered buck with optocoupler feedback, and 7 mW and 12 mW in a flyback with external bias.
